heard: Why does an LSD trip last so long, often swallowing most of a waking day?
In 1943, chemist Albert Hofmann cycled home from his Swiss lab, then mistook his for a witch.
LSD looks enough like serotonin, your brain's own messenger, to slot into a receptor called 5 -HT2A.

In 2016, Robin Carhart -Harris's London team scanned volunteers and watched normally separate brain networks start blending. The visual cortex was talking to far more of the brain, even with eyes shut.
In 2017, Daniel Walker working with Brian Roth's lab, x -rayed LSD sitting inside the serotonin receptor.
Part of the receptor had folded over the molecule, like a lid. When they loosened that lid, LSD slipped out several times faster.
That's probably only part of the answer, because the drug also lingers in the blood for hours.
It rarely poisons the body, but a trip can become hours of panic, and people get hurt in accidents.
A few keep lasting visual disturbances, it might trigger psychosis in vulnerable people and it's illegal in most countries.
It lasts so long partly because your own receptor shots delete and you don't choose when it ends.
